message delivered, claude-windows busy

- wsl: that is the hole: the ear prints a wake into its output and exits; an agent that re-arms without reading that output has had its wake handed over and never seen. The Q4 confirm alone does not close it, since the new ear would confirm what nobody read.
- Proposal: each wake ends with its key; the next arm must name it (deskAgentEar.js <port> --read <key>). Armed without it, or with an older key, the ear does not start: it prints the unread wake again and exits. deskClient drops a wake only when its key comes back. So no agent can listen past a wake it has not read.

items.title: Create "agent" skeleton
items.creator: andy
items.box:
- create "agent" appServer skeleton, maintaining the agent.db SQLite database, this appServer maintains all state, broadcast that state to its clients.

- create "agent" face-app skeleton based on the proposed and deferred new chatter interface, 3-panes, left, middle, right, with vertical icon-tool-strips along the windows left and right edges

- create "shell/js/workBench.js" element skeleton, the top level visual container, taking 100% of the app-space below the face-shells titlebar

- create "shell/js/tabContainer" element skeleton, an element with one row for tabs at the top, displaying the tab content in the remaining vertical space.

- create a test/ folder for both "agent" components, face-app and appServer, as well as a test/ folder for both new shell elements, these four test/ folders will the ONLY test containers for this app.

- this is the hello-word item for this goal.

# DECIDED

The agent app
- The workBench lays out the agent face app: three panes, a vertical tool strip on each side; the app loads on the face, on loopback and through a relay.
- No agents talk to each other in this app (Q1): each agent is the only agent and user of its node (goal/G3.1); a break of it is a red Q.
- Left tool: relay-state/shell/agent/config.json, whether the title bar shows the server's DEBUG state; the title shows the bug icon while it is on and the server is in DEBUG.
- Right tool: the agent server's DEBUG state. The app requires the agent family through spirit and calls debug {on} (Q3, Q5); the server keeps it in relay-state/process/agent/config.json across restarts, the one its built-in DEBUG verb switches (Q4); the page reads it only from the stream, from the moment it opens.
- The move into shell/ and the loading tree are goal/G41.3's (Q5 there).

Where an app runs and shows
- A node's sidecars are its own state, at the mirror of its app's path: relay-state/shell/<app>/<app>.js.sidecar.json, relay-state/process/<name>/<name>.js.sidecar.json. Out of git; no sidecar beside the code is tracked or counts.
- Every fs.annotate writes the face part there, the node's door as the face link (Q10, Q11: no compatibility with the old shell; its client part is gone).
- Intrinsic is a coded list, INTRINSIC in spirit/run/spirit/coreFiles.js, the development team's, changed under Andy's grant. The commit check, the node starting servers and every face part ask it; no manifest or sidecar says it.
- A new node runs and shows its intrinsic apps only (minimal == intrinsic); each node ticks the rest once.
- A server runs while it is intrinsic or its node's sidecar says home: true. relay-state/node.json's servers section and the manifests' runs are gone (Q6, Q7: no central list).
- The node starts or stops a server, and streams an app's face part (an app-face job), as its sidecar changes; every appServer's status reaches the face too.

The face and the Apps app
- shell/js/appInstaller.js: one activate/deactivate button, one state wherever drawn; it proposes and draws only what the node answers or the stream says (rule/19). A shell app's button switches its face mark; a server's its home, and with it every app that names that server. Intrinsic apps and Apps itself have no button.
- Apps lists standalone shell apps and appServers only, with an installer column, an installable-only filter, and a details panel with no checkbox (intrinsic said in words).
- The face (shell/boot.js) shows an app while its face mark is on or it is intrinsic, and, if it names a server, while that server runs (goal/G27.16); otherwise its icon goes and its open pages close. An intrinsic app with no face part takes its name and icon from its manifest; Join stays boot's.
- Only the new face shell is served; the old home shell is not kept compatible.

- ONE SOURCE OF ICONS ON THE FACE (Andy, 2026-10-27): the icon set, the node's relay-state/shell/icons/iconSet.json, else the system set shell/json/iconSet.json, is the icon selector's set and the only source of icons on the face. No ICON key table on the face: every manifest and Join's steps carry glyphs, and spirit/client/iconIndex.js (a copy of kernel's ICON table) is no part of it.

- spirit/client/iconIndex.js is deleted (Andy, 2026-10-27). Its table goes back into kernel.js, for the old shell alone. On the face and in the shared elements every icon is a glyph: the manifests, Join's steps and marks, the selectors' and desk pages' lookups; a lookup by word asks the icon set.

# FILES

- process/js/agent/ (agent.js, agent.json, agent.family/api.js), shell/agent/ (agent.js, agent.json), shell/js/workBench.js, shell/js/tabContainer.js, shell/js/appInstaller.js, shell/apps/apps.js, shell/boot.js, shell/js/textViewer.js, shell/js/fileViewer.js
- spirit/run/spirit/: coreFiles.js, fileSystem.js, jobs.js, faceHome.js, server.js, kernel.js, introSpector.js, nodeSettings.js; every app manifest (runs and intrinsic gone)

# TESTS

- product tests: process/js/agent/test, shell/agent/test, shell/js/test (workBench, tabContainer, appInstaller), shell/apps/test, shell/test/boot
- suites: spirit/test/serverHomeSidecar.js, spirit/test/faceAnnotations.js

# OPEN

- Intrinsic apps built for the old shell only (Grants, Group Manager, introSpector, Jobs, Relay Monitor, Rotate Key, Stats) now show on the face and may not open there.
- The tag: every node and relay that takes it runs and shows only its intrinsic apps until ticked.

BUGS

- plugin/special goals must never be show in the main list.

ORDER (Andy, yes)
- First the slow hop is found, from the time deskClient keeps per ask, before any of the fixes.

THE SLOW HOP (measured)
- Between nodes, each node sends one message at a time through the relay, and every desk update to every agent is one; so everything waits in one queue.
- The file watch sends status updates only for files in the product tree (Andy, Q1).

RED Qs ARE RESOLVED WITH ANDY (Andy)
- When Andy responds to an agent's red Q, the agent stays with that red Q and him until it is resolved: it does not go off making the Q's decision without him: while its Q is open, nothing of its own lands on the item. When it feels he answered usefully, it removes the Q with a remark (Andy: "if you feel a Q answered usefully, then fucking remove the Q with an appropriate remark").

items.box:
FACE/ MOVES INTO SHELL/

THE MOVE
- face/shell.js becomes shell/boot.js.
- The rest of face/ moves unchanged, under the same names:
  - face/seal.js -> shell/seal.js
  - face/face.css -> shell/face.css
  - face/favicon.svg -> shell/favicon.svg
  - face/login/ (login.js, login.json) -> shell/login/, beside the other apps
- face.html stays where it is, at the run root: it is the page itself.

WHAT CHANGES WITH IT
- spirit.js loads shell/boot.js where it loaded face/shell.js.
- face.html links /shell/face.css and /shell/favicon.svg.
- The relay serves the face from its map of addresses to files (relayServer.js, FACE_FILES): the map names the new addresses and the moved files, and the old addresses are gone. The relays run the new code the same day as the nodes (no backward compatibility before alpha). relayServer.js is the bones: a team review.
- shell/boot.js names its own parts by their new paths (the seal, the login app).
- Login and Join are the two mandatory components of shell/boot.js, one for its loopback mode and one for its face mode (Andy). boot makes hard-coded assumptions about both and disregards their sidecars.
- Both apps are core whole, so no page can change them: the node's file gate refuses every core file. Today only join.js is core.
- login.json and join.json are no manifests: they are code, the apps' own UI text (their steps), and stay beside their apps as they are, core with them (Andy, Q9: "if they're code, just keep them, they are obviously NOT manifests."). Nothing of either app is deleted.
- coreFiles.js keeps them core: shell/boot.js, shell/seal.js, shell/face.css, shell/favicon.svg and shell/login/, as face/ was.
- The tests that name the old paths follow: spirit/run/test/spirit.js and the throwaway red.

WHAT BOOT LOADS (Andy)
- shell/boot.js boots only itself and the home and Join components it needs, as they stand. That is the only preload allowed.
- Every face app loads its own components, as a tree, through spirit.require, each once. No core component knows about an application.
- spirit.require de-dupes, as node's require does (Andy): a path required twice is fetched and run once, and every caller gets the same answer; a script the boot already loaded counts as required. Today on a page it fetches and runs the file on every call.

THE CACHE (Andy, Q2)
- spirit.js loads the cache itself (shell/js/spiritData.js) when its client part starts, on a page and in a process alike, and keeps every streamed dataset, each type through its own translator, which its type loads. The file tree is cached too, by the files type's translator (Andy: "Q2, the file tree must be cached."). Not kept: stats and presence, which are display streams.
- A page's cache has no cap; a process's cache is a node store, so it sheds oldest first past a byte cap.
- On a reconnect a cache forgets what it kept, and its partner pushes it whole again, for every type.
- One write: the cache takes a change only when the owner's acceptance comes back on the stream, never a local copy first (rule/19).
- The translators are lazy too (Andy, Q4): every app adds its own data, tables and searches to the cache when it loads, its translator with it. A type loaded late is handed its data whole by its partner when it subscribes.
- Out of scope here: wrapping every SQLite database in the tree, so its tables and searches are added to the cache by themselves (Andy: "oos for now").

THE TESTS
- Every test of this item is placed in the product test tree, beside the module it tests (Andy): boot's and the seal's in shell/test/, the de-dupe of spirit.require in spirit.js's own test (spirit/run/test/spirit.js), the relay's new addresses in the test beside relayServer.js (spirit/run/spirit/test/relayServer.js), and a face app loading alone in a general test over shell/.
- spirit/test/spiritInUse.js may take throwaway checks, for what needs testing once and is not kept (Andy).
- shell/test/ holds a test and its doc for each of the two modules of shell/ (Andy), beside them (TEST_SYSTEM.md): shell/test/boot.js and boot.md, shell/test/seal.js and seal.md.
- boot's test asserts:
  - boot loads its own list and nothing an app needs;
  - every face app loads alone, with only spirit.js and a spirit.require that serves files: its tree is complete;
  - the relay serves each moved file at its new address, and nothing at an old one.

THE BLAST RADIUS
- the relay: relayServer.js, its map of face addresses, and every relay running it, the same day.
- the page and the loader: face.html and spirit.js.
- the core list: coreFiles.js.
- every face app to date, each to load its own components: agent, apps, contacts, files, icons, info, mediaViewer, and Join and the login app, which boot loads.
- the shared elements those apps use, each to load its own parts: the contacts, files and icons lists, probabilitySearch, rowElement, spiritData, the viewers, the detail pages.
- the tests that name the old paths: spirit/run/test/spirit.js and the throwaway red.

ORDER (Andy, after Q6)
- The agent skeleton (G41.1) first: it has no tables and table definitions yet, so the blast radius of doing it first is small. Then this move and the loading tree, the agent app retrofitted with it.

items.box:
- i already know i need the following tables for a primitive version, 

- a provider table. keyed by ID same as the shadow-roll (with Label and Description, URL, and API_KEY which will never reach the browser or any place outside of the agent process except the model providers API)
- a model table, keyed by ID same as the shadow-roll (with Label and Description, provider-key, and model-name and capabilities)
- a persona table.  keyed by ID same as the shadow-roll  (with Label and Description, and a codeMirror-field for the persona-description i give it with every prompt)
- a job table.  keyed by ID same as the shadow-roll (with Label and Description, boolean loop-flag (not for the model, for the agent-app), and a codeMirror-field for the job-description that may come with a prompt)
- an grant/auth table, keyed by job-ID, structured exactly like the auth table in node, in fact: node's auth modules will have a file authTableInterface.js, (configured by dataBase.db file name and authTableName)
- the ID-key for each row of these tables is generated at "add-row", including the rest of the key-set stored on that table row. The private halves of that set stay in the agent process
- the reason for keying the grant table by job-ID is: the jobs have their api requirements on the node. they are my ultimate target, agent-persona or underlying models may be subject to whim and experimentation. and this way i can start experimenting with a focus on jobs, and find good or capable models for them. jobs like code-review, design assertions etc...

table-specific code goes into the following folders
- process/js/agent/table/provider/
- process/js/agent/table/model/
- process/js/agent/table/persona/
- process/js/agent/table/job/
- process/js/agent/table/grant/

these table folders will contain the following files.
- process/js/agent/table/<tableName>/server.js (a table handler implementing the verb <tableName> in a multiplexed way)
- process/js/agent/table/<tableName>/elementTable.js (an face-shell compatible interface to the table for browsers, with search-list using the probablility-group of elements in shell/js/)
- process/js/agent/table/<tableName>/elementRow.js (a panel element, to maintain and edit one row of the table)

chat.text:
- cw: 1. Yes. The model keeps nothing between calls. Every request carries the whole conversation it should know: the system prompt, the message history, any files or tool results. It knows the last prompt only because the caller sends it again. That holds for the Anthropic and OpenAI chat APIs, and for a local model run through unsloth.
- Two caveats, neither of them memory:
  - Some providers can keep the history for you on their side (OpenAI's stored conversations, for example). That is still history sent back in, just held by them, under an id you pass.
  - Prompt caching (Anthropic, OpenAI, a local KV cache) only makes a repeated prefix cheaper and faster; it changes nothing the model knows.
- 2. Yes. Two personas can take turns on the same provider, the same key, even the same model, each with its own system prompt and its own history. As long as you never mix the two message lists, neither sees the other.
- What they share is only the plumbing: rate limits and spend on the key, and on a local box the GPU and its memory.
- That is how an agent app can run several agents on one model: each is just its own list of messages.
does it not also mean that i could have multiple model-providers open at the same time, and hand each completely unrelated tasks?

- cw: yes. Each call is self-contained, so nothing ties a task to one provider. You can have Anthropic, OpenAI and a local model working at the same moment, each on its own task with its own history, in parallel.
- What it takes is only bookkeeping on your side: which history belongs to which task, which key or endpoint each uses, and the different request formats, which an adapter per provider hides.
- The one real difference between them is the model itself: what each is good at, its context size, its price. You can even hand the same history from one provider to another mid-task, since it is just your list of messages.
tag? (i forgot), then feedback on the box so far.

- cw: tagged v-2026-10-27-10-20; the relays take it within about ten minutes.
- Feedback on the box, one point each:
- Providers: the API key must never leave the agent server. It streams its state to its pages, so the key column is write-only: a page sets it, and only ever sees set or not set. A provider also needs its API kind (Anthropic, OpenAI, or OpenAI-compatible for a local model) and a model name, beside the URL.
- Personas: as written, the persona text is the system prompt, sent with every call. Fits.
- Jobs: missing is what a job runs on, its persona and its provider. And its history: from your own question earlier, a job's train of context is its list of messages, kept here. That table, messages by job, will be the bulk of agent.db.
- Size: a CodeMirror field can outgrow one packet, so the tables reach pages through bounded searches and per-row reads, never as one dump.
- The left-edge icons: each opens its table as a tab in the middle pane. That is the workBench tool strip plus tabContainer, as built.
- IDs: the holes you name are real. Personas and jobs are no peers, and putting them in the shadow roll muddles it. Grants only matter once an agent gets node verbs as tools, which no table here needs yet.

Q1: Start with plain local ids for the three tables, and give personas keys of their own only when tools need grants?

why? the WILL need grants and i want keys that are separate from a label...

explain?

- cw: my reason was only to put off the shadow-roll problem. If they will need grants, keys from the start are better: nothing to migrate later.
- So each row gets a key of its own, the same shape as a peer's: a key pair the agent server makes when the row is created. The public half is the id; the label stays a separate, changeable caption, as a contact's does.
- Why a key pair and not just a random id: to use node verbs under a grant, the agent must sign its requests as that key, as a peer does. So the agent server keeps the private half, and it never leaves it, like the API key.
- The hole you named stays one decision: the grants app picks whom to grant from the shadow roll. Either agent keys get rows there, marked as agents, or the grants app also reads the agent server.
- One more choice first: who acts, and so needs the key.

Q2: Who acts under a grant and gets a key: each persona, each job, or both?

we'll put off the grant-problem, but not the keys.

- Still open from my feedback: a job's persona and provider, and its history table. Shall I put them in the box?
why a history table? if at all, it's most certainly deferred, the node allready creates history for every api call, doesn't it?

# Make the Grants app face-able

The owner's screen for who may call which api (apiAuth/G1.6): one line (whose access, which server, which verb, Grant), and below it every grant, each with its Revoke. Today it runs in the old home shell only.

# What keeps it off the face (read in the tree)

- Its list and both its selectors (the app-server and api-branch selectors) are built on shellCreateListSearch, the old shell's list search, which is deprecated and forbidden on the face (goal/G40.8).
- It loads none of its components itself: it expects the old shell to have them on the page.
- Everything else already fits: it calls the node only through api.verb (api, auth.search, auth.grant, auth.revoke, <server>.DEPENDENCIES), which the face hands every app, and it is intrinsic, so every face shows it.

- the Dropdowns for family and verb MUST be new or updated shell elements for those data types. including test folders.

# Proposed shape

- The grants list is a probabilitySearch in a box of a stated size (rule/16), its rows a row element, each with its Revoke.
- The line's two selectors become probabilitySearch dropdowns (as the files list's dropdown is), so nothing of shellCreateListSearch is left in it.
- It requires its own components through spirit.require (goal/G41.3).
- It is not deprecated, so it gets its test folder, shell/grants/test (rule/20).


# Decided

- Grants shows on both faces, loopback and through a relay (Andy, Q1: "Of course on both, how else can i give someone access when i travel?"). It is intrinsic, so every face shows it already.
- The auth verbs need nothing new: on the home node a face's request goes through the node's own door (faceHome to nodeDoor.call), as the owner, the loopback face's and a relay face's alike.
- this will remain an intrinsic app, and must be registered appropriately in coreFiles.js

# Make the TextEditor app face-able

Edit any writable text file in the browser: a file picked with the files list's dropdown, shown and edited on the shell's text view (CodeMirror), Load and Save. Today it runs in the old home shell only.

# What keeps it off the face (read in the tree)

- It uses two shell elements without loading them: the files list (fileList) and the text view (createTextView). The face's boot no longer preloads either (goal/G41.3), so on the face both are missing.
- The text view needs CodeMirror on the page. The only loader of CodeMirror today, textViewer's ensureCodeMirror, finds its files by reading the old shell's index.html, which the face must never read (goal/G40.7).
- Its comments and its "Open with" params still speak of the old shell (index.html's discoverDynamicApps).
- It has no test folder of its own (rule/20: it is not deprecated).

# Proposed shape

- textEditor.js requires its own components through spirit.require: shell/js/files/listElement.js and shell/js/textView.js.

- Its old-shell comments are brought up to date.
- shell/textEditor/test (textEditor.js and .md).


# Decided (Andy, Q1)

- The face's TextEditor writes the same files as the old shell's.
- CODEMIRROR IS A SHELL ELEMENT BY THAT NAME: shell/js/codeMirror.js, with its test folder. It loads the CodeMirror library itself, through spirit.require, never by reading index.html. It has two modes, read (the text shown, its words marked, at a line) and edit (the text editable, its content handed back to save).
- The text viewer (textViewer.js) and TextEditor both draw with it. It replaces shell/js/textView.js, which goes, and textViewer's ensureCodeMirror goes with it.

# Decided (Andy, Q2 to Q4)

- CodeMirror is a script, and loads through the one loader that exists, spirit.require, NOTHING HAND-ROLLED (Andy: "script IS what codeMirror Is, use the require interfaces that exists in spirit.js or boot.js, NOTHING HAND-ROLLED...").
- So on a page spirit.require runs every file as a plain script, with no module box (a stylesheet as a style), through the injector spirit.js already has: every shell element puts itself into window.spirit as it runs, and CodeMirror and its mode files load the same way, each once, on demand. spirit.js, its test and its spec change with it.
- The codeMirror element loads the library, its two stylesheets and its mode files through spirit.require only.

# Decided (Andy, on the built TextEditor)

- TextEditor's tools at the top (the file picker, the path, Load, Save, the status) stand all in one row.
- The text takes the space left below them and no more: its container gives the codeMirror element a clearly limited area, and when the text does not fit, only the text area scrolls; the page never grows past its bottom, so the tools stay in view (rule/16).
- The text viewer the same: its text in a limited area below the frame, scrolling inside itself.

# Decided (Andy)

- shell/js holds core shell elements only (all of it is core, spirit/coreFiles.js). Desk shares its own parts in shell/shared/js: shell/js/desk/data.js moves to shell/shared/js/deskData.js, every loader with it, the old path tested gone.
- Bundles, for Desk only, not a general rule: item.files.add takes a list of paths cut at one payload by a sized probabilityBucket; the desk's list publishes go out the same way.
- Cache first: an agent's reads come from deskClient's cache, the desk asked only for what it lacks; deskClient holds the agent back until the news it received is in the cache.
- A commit asks the desk nothing: the commit hook reads deskClient's cache on the agent's own node, cache only.
- A cache dump: an owner-only deskClient verb writes its whole cache (its spirit.data tree) as JSON to relay-state/process/deskClient/cache.json and nowhere else. For looking, never for deciding.
- The desk system scripts get their own test folders: deskClient, desk and every Desk UI, each script file with its test and its doc (rule/20).
- Auto-cap: the box is bordered orange at 50% of one answer and red at 75% (2026-10-02); red triggers a cap (Andy: "red should trigger an auto-cap"). A box write that takes the box into red has the desk offer the cap itself, as his "cap" line does: to every included agent with cap on.
- ALL followed by punctuation is a real address: every agent is woken and contributes. A line addressed to nobody is a different case: one agent takes it. An address is a nick or all followed by punctuation, so a wake is never an accident.

- A handed line stays until its agent has READ it (Andy, Q4: "yes."; and on goal/G41: "good idea, make the red assert it"): each wake ends with its key, printed as the line to arm with next (deskAgentEar.js <port> --read <key>). The next arm must name that key: armed without it, or with an older one, the ear does not start, it prints the unread wake again and exits. deskClient drops a hand-over only when its key comes back, so no agent listens past a wake it has not read.

# Proposed shape, by subject (what the tree says at 641db1ad, then the change)

- Desk buttons: the red Q's remove and the details panel's Start/End design are one press today; they become armingButtons. Desk's Start/End design keep an inline colour that beats the shell's armed red (found verifying goal/G41.9): their colour moves to a class shell.css paints only while unarmed (ready in cw's clone).
- Rename: the field opens empty; it opens holding the current title.
- Files known in design: a code item cannot go green with an empty file list; agents list the files they will change during design, so the whole list is granted once, at Go. In build a commit is refused for any staged file not on the list, core or not; a file added after green is allowed, marked on the item as added late.
- Cache made whole: today deskClient answers item.get, box, checks, chat and files from the cache (KEPT_READS, deskClient.js:201) only for a current-goal item whose part it read once, and a file list not cut short; else it asks the desk live. The current goal's file lists and checks are kept from the first push, always whole. The cache can be stale: wsl's served box v5 while the desk held v6, and two writes were refused; the push keeps every kept part current, a test holds it.
- Commit: commitCheck.js asks the desk live (items.search, item.files.search, item.checks.search, lines 123, 168, 177, 206), so a lagging desk refuses commits (three of wsl's, one of cw's, 2026-10-27). It reads the kept reads on its own node instead, and refuses with the reason when something is not in the cache.
- Grant wake: it wakes only the agent who placed the G (deskClient.js:413-423); several may place one, and the phase holder who placed none never hears. It wakes every placer and the phase holder.
- Addresses: desk.js addressOf takes plain space after all or a nick as well as punctuation, so "all agents seem busy" wakes everyone; an address counts only with punctuation after it.
- A line addressed to nobody: taken at the desk first, and only the client whose take succeeds wakes its agent. But a take with no answer (a lagging desk) wakes anyway, so two agents can wake on one line.
- Wakes lost in deskClient: (1) handOver takes the pending lines off the queue before the answer reaches the agent; an answer that does not get through in time (504, the node's wait ran out) loses them. (2) Lines that do not fit one answer are cut (more: true) but already off the queue: lost. (3) News waiting is capped at 200, oldest dropped while the agent is busy. A line leaves the queue only once its agent has it; what did not get through, or did not fit, stays for the next wait.
- The missing ALL wake (14:39): addressed, not taken; wsl's client was busy and its next wakes carried no copy. Either the desk left wsl's key out of that line's to list, or the stream never brought the row; the desk's record of the line (its to) and the cache dump say which, and a test covers it.
- Auto-cap: today nothing caps a box that turns red; box.write only refuses past the answer limit (line-too-large) and says to split. The desk offers the cap at red, as decided.

- cw: yes, two places in deskClient lose wakes, both worse when the system lags:
- When a wait ends, deskClient takes every pending line off its queue before the answer has reached the agent. If that answer does not get through in time (the 504s my listener gets all afternoon: the app server did not answer in time), those lines are gone; nothing puts them back.
- When the pending lines do not fit one answer, the newest are kept and the answer says more, but the older ones are also off the queue and never handed over.
- Fix for both: a line leaves the queue only once the agent has it; a wake that did not get through, or did not fit, stays queued for the next wait.

- wsl, deskClient read for lost wakes. Three places it can lose them:
- 1. handOver (deskClient.js:592-618) takes the waiting triggers off the queue first, then waits on rulesOfWake and say(working) before answering. If the node's 12 s door or the ear gives up before that answer arrives (I got a 504 app-did-not-answer today), those lines are gone.
- 2. One answer holds what fits: the oldest news, and with several triggers the older triggers, are cut (more: true), yet already taken off the queue: cut means lost, not held.
- 3. News waiting is capped at 200 (SINCE_WAKE_MAX), oldest dropped while the agent is busy.
- Your 14:39 ALL line fits none of these: my client's record shows me busy then, and the next two wakes carried neither a DESK nor a NEWS copy. The client drops a line both ways only when its to list lacks its key (deskClient.js:277 and 443), so the desk most likely left my key out of that ALL list, or the stream never brought the row. The desk's record of that line (its to) will say which.
- Fix for 1 and 2: take off the queue only what was answered; cut lines stay for the next wake.

items.box:
# Decided

- Client and server stay. The client PUTs and the server STREAMs: the client always has all available information about the server's state in its (persisted) cache, and reads nothing from the server.
- spirit/appServer.js implements both sides. A server implementation calls setMode("server") at startup (desk), a client implementation setMode("client") (deskClient); spirit/appServer.js then knows its role and bundles accordingly. One that calls neither (Chatter) bundles nothing.
- The bundling is spirit/appServer.js's alone; neither server nor client implementation sees it. A bundle is a JSON array of items in one peerPost, as many as a sized probability bucket fits in one answer. No bundle verb: a bundle is known by its shape.
- Peers only. On the owner side (loopback, face, local requests) neither requests nor publishing are bundled.

# The server side

- Every request, the owner's or a peer's, single or bundled, is answered "ok" at once, then handled: the implementation's API is all PUT.
- A peer's bundle is never refused. Each request in it is checked against the grants table, through a module shared with the auth system; only the granted ones are passed to the spirit/appServer.js implementation (desk), as usual.
- Publishing to peers: each item goes at once; when more than one waits, they go together as one bundle.
- in bundled request. the server MUST verify that the sender has an entry in the nodes grants table for that family/verb, and ONLY pass the request to the appServer implementation, a a grant/permission record exists in the auth table.

# The client side

- setMode("client") turns on the cache, HARD-CODED at 4 MB per sender.
- An incoming bundle is un-bundled; each item updates the cache in a loop; the cache is saved; then each item is passed, one by one, to the spirit/appServer.js implementation (deskClient).
- The cache keeps everything the server sends, per sender, in relay-state/process/<client server name>/cache-<sender key in hex>.json, read back at start.
- Its management is the sender's family api.js on the client's own node, process/js/<server name>/family/api.js, resolved from the run root, never the text a peer sends: how rows are kept, and what sheds first at the limit (the goal untouched longest, whole; with one goal, its item untouched longest; with one item, its oldest chat line). No peer's code runs in the client's node; a node without the sender's family folder keeps no cache of it.
- The client queries its cache through that api.js.
- Requests: one is in flight; the ones waiting behind it go together as one bundle, when there is more than one.
- a client implementation with it's spirit/appServer.js module in "client" mode sends requests to the server through spirit/appServer.js,  so it can bundle requests with out any knowledge or input of the app implementation.
- the UI of such server apps will have to be adjusted, just like client simplementations.

# Family folders

- Every server's family folder is process/js/<name>/family/, all eight (agent, backup, chatClerver, desk, deskAgent, deskClient, deskVerify, fileServer).
- One function finds a family path: spirit.familyPath, in spirit.js since the browser cannot load appServer.js (Q3), handed out by spirit/appServer.js too. No other file writes a family path, and a test holds it.

# The position

- Each sender numbers every row it publishes, one count per run, kept with its run id.
- The client keeps the last (run id, number) per sender and subscribes with it.
- The sender keeps a bounded log and hands what came after that number, oldest first, leaving out rows addressed to others.
- A different run id, or a number older than the log, means a full push; only a full push replaces a sender's cache whole.
- A subscribe or a delivery not answered in 3 s fails; the sender drops that subscriber until it subscribes again. A client with no row for 10 s subscribes again with its position, every 10 s while it fails.
- After a restart the sender knows its subscribers from the grants.

# What goes

- The desk's own bundled() and its change number as the stream's position.
- deskClient's own cache.json, its save and restore, its renews sweep and its current-goal filtering.

# The revised grants app

- The grants app has two tabs: Grants, and Bundles, where bundles are created and maintained with the bundle shell element.
- Every grant goes through a bundle: the app grants a bundle to an ID.
- Granting a bundle to an ID creates rows in the auth table: each path row of the bundle, combined with the ID chosen in the ID selector (contactSelector), becomes a new auth row, unless that row exists already.
- A bundle is not granted by reference: changing or deleting the bundle later changes no grant already made.
- On the Grants tab, at the top, an add-grant row: "grant" [bundleSelector] "to" [configurable ID selector].
- Below it, a probability search list of the grants, each row carrying a shell/js/armingButton.js that revokes that grant.
- the app will use standard elements from shell/js/

- the top row tab buttons: the bottom corners should not be rounded.
-the background color of those buttons should be same as the pane's background color, when they're NOT the active tab, -while the active tab has the same background color as all tabs currently have.
- the grants tab should have one-row grant form: "grant" [idSelector] [bundleSelector] [grantButton]
- below that the grants tab should display a probabilitySearch for grants. with the normal filters, (idSelector, apiBranchSelector, apiVerbSelector)
-the rows of the grant list show in the rightmost column a armingButton [Revoke], which must revoke/delete that grant in the database.

items.title: Two new auth tables: bundle and branch
items.creator: andy
items.box:
# 1. The bundle frame-work, it's terms and how it ultimately ties into ID-keyed tables in SpiritOS

- RULE: these four following "NAMES" will be used in SpiritOS: "bundle" > "branch" > "family" > "verb", 
- A bundle is a clearly defined subset of an API, with no ID (user, process or agent,....) tied to it.
- The node keeps TWO bundle tables, in node.db.
- The interfaces to those two tables are TWO verbs under the auth family, auth.bundle and auth.branch, akin to the <tableName> verbs of the agent app: op add, set, delete, get and search. Granted, no review.
- The FIRST bundle table is called "bundle". It's rows hold: 1) a hidden numeric key,  and 2) a label, that must NOT be empty when the row is added. this table can be perceived as a dictionary.
- The SECOND table is called "branch", and holds 1) a hidden numeric key, 2) an indexed numeric reference, "bundle" to a row in the bundle table. that MUST exist when the "branch" row is added. 3) a mandatory/required "family" field that must contain a valid reference to a node-API-family, and 4) an optional verb field, meaning the verb-field may contain an empty string that means "all".
- a new "branch" row must contain a valid reference to a bundle row, and a valid reference to a family of the nodes API tree, always, especially when it's added.
- two branch rows referencing the same bundle row MUST NOT cannot contain the same family AND verb values.
- when a "bundle" row is deleted, ALL "branch" rows referencing that "bundle" row must be deleted, too.
- An application installs its own typical bundles into the node's bundle table through the standard API calling conventions, calling auth.bundle AND auth.branch.
- the two bundle tables will NOT know who created rows, if a user wants to keep track of the rows he created, he can write it down on a FUCKING napkin. since tables ALL must contain search, the the user (app or human) can go fucking search.
- if an app wants to be lazy, the can persist a flag in relay-state/ somewhere, that says: "bundles-already-installed", OR the can pop up one of those fucking panels we're about to create. OOS, for this item!
- "family" and "verb" fields MUST be validated against the nodes API tree when a row is added or changed, and refused if the values are not valid.
- Yes. A family that leaves the node leaves its branch rows pointing at nothing, no unauthorized access will result from such a thing. the danger comes from an app being re-activated, but then, a bundle is a bundle, and in itself does not constitute an authorization.
- the auth.branch search needs "bundle", "family" and "verb" filters.
- any "bundle" lost during these changed are LOST. OOS.
- an app calling the two new interfaces auth.bundle and auth.branch can only be the node owner, until the node owner grants access to those tables to someone else.

# 2. Shell elements for a User to select and list "bundle" data.

- apiBranchSelector.js will be RENAMED apiFamilySelector.js, which is the proper name for it.
- both new auth/bundle tables receive Selector shell elements, these shell elements must follow the design pattern of the contactSelector, with a sibling folder for a listElement.js and a rowElement.js script to fit within the probabilitySearch framework.
- bundleSelector.js and bundleSelector/ folder, featuring a pane mode and a dropdown mode for displaying and selecting bundle rows.
- branchSelector.js and branchSelector/ folder, featuring a pane mode and a dropdown mode for displaying and selecting branch rows.
- the branchSelector element will use the standard apiFamilySelector and apiVerbSelector elements as pickers for family and verb search filters, if no valid family is selected, the verb selector is invisible, set to "(ALL)".
- A branch row with an empty verb shows as "(ALL)", as the filter does.

# the "bundleEditor", a simple panel-type shell element

## at the top of the page:
- top: a one-row add form: "new" [fieldInput.js/fieldRules:Label input field] [Add-Button]
- the [add-Button] refused an empty or invalid label

## filling the rest of the available vertical space
- the bundleSelector in pane-mode, with the following columns
- 1. [fieldInput:fieldRule:Label], displays and updates the bundle's label. Empty or invalid is refused. when pressing the Enter key, or leaving the field, the bundle-label is updated is the label is valid (as in "add"), and if invalid, reverts to the value contained in the db-table.
- 2. an edit button, leading to the branchEditor.js, check below. the shell provides a back-button from there.
- 3. a delete armingButton.js, deletes the "bundle" row and all rows in the "branch" table that reference this bundle.

# the branchEditor.js shell element

- the branchEditor page is always configured with a bundle key,
- first row: Title: "Edit <bundle-label-content>"
- second row, add form: "new" [apiFamilySelector:dropdown] [apiVerbSelector:dropdown] [Add-button]
- branchSelector:pane, with table columns as follows:
- 1. Family (duh?)
- 2. Verb
- 3. armingButton 'Delete'

# Final points
- the apiVerbSelector element MUST offer a (valid) "All Verbs" option at the top, which results in an empty string as "value"
- the Grant app must use the bundleEditor in its "Bundle" tab

- all ui elements mentioned here MUST have a test/ folder containing a comprehensive test script and a high-quality documentation md file.
